{"id": "9:103/q26", "question": "Is prayer for a charity donor required of the collector or recipient?", "turns_on": "The imperative's force and whether donor request, type of gift, or recipient's office changes it.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q26/p1", "position": "The prayer is recommended, not required.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī argues God rewards charity, not the collector; al-Ālūsī prefers recommendation in all cases. The Prophet's practice establishes it as the collector's sunnah in al-Nasafī and others."}, {"id": "9:103/q26/p2", "position": "The collector or imam must pray for the donor.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī cites the imperative's apparent force; al-Baghawī records the duty. Bashīr ibn al-Khaṣāṣiyya even advises those overcharged by collectors to gather assets and obtain their prayer."}, {"id": "9:103/q26/p3", "position": "It is required for obligatory zakat but recommended for voluntary charity.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and al-Ālūsī report this reverse distinction."}, {"id": "9:103/q26/p4", "position": "It is required of the ruler but recommended of a poor recipient.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says presenting to the ruler displays obedience deserving thanks; al-Baghawī records the same division."}, {"id": "9:103/q26/p5", "position": "It is required for voluntary charity but recommended for obligatory zakat.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī records this distinction."}, {"id": "9:103/q26/p6", "position": "It is recommended for a donor to the ruler but required of a poor recipient.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says the poor recipient has not been individually designated."}, {"id": "9:103/q26/p7", "position": "It is required when the donor asks, recommended otherwise.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī gives this sixth view; Abū Awfā requested prayer in one report."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q27", "question": "Was the command to pray for them abrogated?", "turns_on": "Whether 9:84 addresses the same persons and practice as 9:103.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q27/p1", "position": "It was abrogated by the prohibition on prayer over dead hypocrites in 9:84.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and al-Qurṭubī transmit this claim; some link it to the Prophet's special status and 24:63."}, {"id": "9:103/q27/p2", "position": "It was not abrogated; prayer for repentant donors remains.", "reasons": "Scholars cited by al-Naḥḥās point to the Prophet's repeated donor prayers; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says 9:84 concerns unbelieving hypocrites whereas these were repentant believers. Al-Qurṭubī says Muslims follow the Prophet's practice."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q28", "question": "May the blessing formula be used for people besides the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether Prophetic donor prayers establish a general formula or his standing makes it exclusive.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q28/p1", "position": "Prayer and blessing for donors or other Muslims are permitted.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says the Prophet is an exemplar, citing donor and Jābir reports. Al-Qāḍī cites the taught blessing on Muḥammad's family as including ʿAlī. The Shīʿa invoke blessings for ʿAlī and descendants, arguing 9:103 permits blessing payers and returned greetings are accepted. Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī are reported by the Study Quran to reject exclusivity."}, {"id": "9:103/q28/p2", "position": "The formula 'God's blessings upon him' is reserved for the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to prohibit ṣalāt for anyone else; al-Rāzī's school and some commentators restrict it. Al-Qurṭubī reports appeal to the Prophet's special standing in 24:63. The Study Quran says Muslims invoke blessings and peace on Muḥammad but only peace on other prophets."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q29", "question": "How is the greeting of peace analyzed in the discussion of blessings?", "turns_on": "The grammatical structure, word order, and purpose of the greeting.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q29/p1", "position": "'Peace be upon you' can have an indefinite subject with 'upon you' as predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the indefinite is qualified by complete peace, citing 2:221 and 2:96; alternatively 'upon you' qualifies the subject and the predicate is omitted for grandeur. He says indefinite salām has fuller qualities than definite al-salām, with Qurʾanic comparisons and Yaḥyā as an exception."}, {"id": "9:103/q29/p2", "position": "The reversed reply 'and upon you, peace' foregrounds what concerns the respondent.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says speakers put the most important element first; al-Rāzī adds that it promises more and reads 4:86 as support."}, {"id": "9:103/q29/p3", "position": "Greeting with peace reassures a person amid pervasive potential harm and creates a spiritual bond.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī argues restraint of harm preserves safety more generally than adding benefit; unknown creatures naturally elicit flight. The plural can include guardian angels and different spirit classes. Mutual spiritual reflection explains a student's greeting and prayer for a teacher."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q30", "question": "What hermeneutic principle governs a legal and an ordinary sense of a word here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q30/p1", "position": "When ordinary linguistic and legal senses are equally plausible, the legal sense takes priority absent contextual evidence.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān orders legal over customary over linguistic use. Al-Itqān says ijtihād clarifies general wording, ambiguous points, and legal rulings; scholars must use evidence rather than mere opinion, and this verse's prayer serves as an example of the legal-versus-linguistic choice."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q31", "question": "What does the prayer command imply for funeral prayer?", "turns_on": "Whether 9:103's prayer includes funeral practice and how that practice is historically grounded.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q31/p1", "position": "Funeral prayer is prescribed as a communal obligation, alongside washing and burial duties.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī cites al-Kāfī's use of the verse and a report to pray over righteous and sinful dead; he says it became obligatory in year one after the Prophet prayed four takbīrs at Barāʾ ibn Maʿrūr's grave. Al-Qunya treats denial of its obligation as unbelief. Washing is communal duty; intention is not required for validity, though it discharges duty. He says death makes the body impure and washing honors it, even if found in water."}, {"id": "9:103/q31/p2", "position": "Adam's funeral establishes ancient precedent for washing, shrouding, prayer, burial and laḥd.", "reasons": "One report has angels wash and pray; another has Seth lead thirty takbīrs after Gabriel declined. Al-Bursevī says pre-Islamic Arabs may have washed and shrouded bodies and recited virtues, reconciling reports that funeral prayer is unique to this community."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q32", "question": "How is the reply in al-Aʿshā's cited prayer verse parsed?", "turns_on": "The case assigned to the reply in the poetic citation.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q32/p1", "position": "The reply can be nominative like a greeting returned with 'peace be upon you'.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda's citation treats the answer as a nominal expression."}, {"id": "9:103/q32/p2", "position": "The reply can be accusative as an imperative to repeat the same words and pray.", "reasons": "Al-Majāz reports another reading of the poetic line."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q33", "question": "What does God's ṣalāt mean when attributed to Him?", "turns_on": "Whether God's ṣalāt is described as an idiom of desert or as mercy.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q33/p1", "position": "It describes persons deserving divine blessing, not God supplicating for them.", "reasons": "Sībawayh's idiom compares 'woe to the deniers' in 52:11 and 37:12 and 'woe to the defrauders' in 83:1; al-Ṭabrisī applies this account to God's prayer on His Messenger."}, {"id": "9:103/q33/p2", "position": "God's prayer signifies mercy, while the Prophet's prayer is supplication.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes the subjects and compares 9:99."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q34", "question": "Why does the verse state that his prayer is a comfort after commanding it?", "turns_on": "The causal and emphatic functions of inna.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q34/p1", "position": "The inna-clause gives the reason for the command and answers an implied 'why?'.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān says explicit causes strengthen and help transmit rules, and causal fāʾ could replace inna while losing the question-answer effect; al-Itqān cites Ibn Jinnī's 'because' sense. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the clause explanation of the imperative."}, {"id": "9:103/q34/p2", "position": "The emphatic clause confirms the significance of the preceding commands.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī compares other inna confirmations, including Luqmān's counsel and passages in 22:1, 31:17, 11:37 and 12:53."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q35", "question": "How does the pronoun of the affair interact with emphatic inna?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q35/p1", "position": "In conditional clauses, a pronoun of the affair is scarcely used without inna.", "reasons": "ʿAbd al-Qāhir cites 12:90, 9:63, 6:54, 23:117 and 22:46; even if Abū al-Ḥasan's forward reference to al-abṣār in 22:46 is allowed, he rejects a version lacking inna. He notes 112:1's exceptional ungoverned pronoun and possible non-affair parse."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q36", "question": "How is 'your prayer' read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted forms and whether singular or plural better conveys generic prayer or many prayers.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q36/p1", "position": "The plural ṣalawātuka is read, indicating repeated supplications or multiple recipients.", "reasons": "Medinan readers and most named canonical readers including Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, plus Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb, read the plural, with kasra on tāʾ. Abū Ḥātim prefers it and denies feminine plural implies few, citing 18:109 and 31:27; al-Jishumī favors its transmission by most readers and the two sanctua

{"id": "9:103/q37", "question": "What does 'sakan for them' signify?", "turns_on": "Whether sakan names emotional assurance, mercy, dignity, nearness, purification, or inner stillness.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q37/p1", "position": "The Prophet's prayer gives calm, reassurance, security, and confidence that God accepted repentance or charity.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī, al-Kalbī and many later readers connect repose to accepted repentance or charity; some call it safety or strengthening of hearts. Ibn ʿĀshūr defines sakan as what one rests in, figurative mental calm, comparing night, home and spouse in 6:96 and 16:80; he also says it inclines the soul to righteous action, comparing 9:45 and 13:28. Al-Ālūsī prefers making prayer itself tranquility by hyperbole over likening resort to it to a home; al-Rāzī's soul-transmission account is rejected as philosophical by Ibn al-Naqīb."}, {"id": "9:103/q37/p2", "position": "It is mercy for them.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās repeatedly gives this gloss; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ṭabrisī and others report it. Some connect it to God's response to the prayer."}, {"id": "9:103/q37/p3", "position": "It gives dignity, composure, gravitas, or honor.", "reasons": "Qatāda consistently gives this gloss; al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others preserve it."}, {"id": "9:103/q37/p4", "position": "It is nearness to God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās through al-Ḍaḥḥāk gives this in al-Māwardī and Ibn al-Jawzī; Abū Ḥayyān includes nearness."}, {"id": "9:103/q37/p5", "position": "It purifies them.", "reasons": "Muʿādh is cited in al-Thaʿlabī, repeated by Ibn al-Jawzī."}, {"id": "9:103/q37/p6", "position": "In an inward reading it is spiritual tranquility from Prophetic attention.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī describes a settled light strengthening certainty and freeing the heart from egoic and satanic agitation; al-Sulamī says it cuts worldly attachment and turns one to the afterlife."}, {"id": "9:103/q37/p7", "position": "The Prophet's radiant soul affects and elevates the repentants' souls through prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives this philosophical account; Ibn al-Naqīb rejects it as unsuitable to Qurʾanic exegesis."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q38", "question": "How is the word 'sakan' read or construed?", "turns_on": "The noun's active or passive force and a consonantal reading variant.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q38/p1", "position": "It is an active sense: something that calms them.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn favors this because the verse says 'for them'; a passive noun would normally require 'to it'. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the wording metonymy for the cause of tranquility."}, {"id": "9:103/q38/p2", "position": "It is a passive-form noun, like a thing spent or broken.", "reasons": "Abū al-Baqāʾ explains its masculine form this way; al-Bursevī repeats a passive-form analogy."}, {"id": "9:103/q38/p3", "position": "A reading gives the kāf of sakan sukūn.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports the variant."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q39", "question": "What does the final statement say God hears and knows?", "turns_on": "Whether the closing attributes refer chiefly to the penitents' speech or the Prophet's supplication.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q39/p1", "position": "He hears the penitents' request, confession, repentance and speech, and knows their remorse, intentions, grief and sincerity.", "reasons": "Muqātil emphasizes their request to have wealth accepted; al-Ṭabarī includes all creatures' speech, and al-Wāḥidī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Qāshānī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Bursevī and others specify remorse. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says this reassures all hearers charged with duties."}, {"id": "9:103/q39/p2", "position": "He hears the Prophet's prayer and knows its object, worthiness, reforming intent and wise response.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī includes what the Prophet seeks for them, Ibn Kathīr says God knows who deserves it, and Ibn ʿĀshūr says hearing hints at answering prayer and knowing at its good effect. Al-Biqāʿī stresses the Prophet's sincerity; al-Ālūsī adds the divine wisdom required."}, {"id": "9:103/q39/p3", "position": "He hears their confession and knows how they handle charity.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī gives this paired explanation."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q40", "question": "How does the command connect to the surrounding verses?", "turns_on": "Whether the connection is the penitents' practical repair, visible obedience, or a wider closing summary.", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q40/p1", "position": "It follows the confession and repentance in 9:102 and repairs the missed Tabūk contribution.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says repentance repairs what can be repaired: they missed fighting and spending, and Tabūk depleted communal funds. Al-Biqāʿī sees the partial taking as compassionate confirmation of acceptance. Al-Rāzī's expiation advocates argue a new general zakat order would interrupt this link; zakat advocates answer that willing payment tests repentance."}, {"id": "9:103/q40/p2", "position": "It relates to the visible duties by which belief can be known, unlike concealed hypocrisy.", "reasons": "Al-Karmānī and Durra al-Tanzīl contrast inward hypocrisy known to God and outward obedience seen by God, the Messenger and believers."}, {"id": "9:103/q40/p3", "position": "The final names confirm the prayer's rationale and may conclude the preceding two verses.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī offers both scopes for the closure."}]}
{"id": "9:103/q41", "question": "What does the verse suggest about repentance and inward reform?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "9:103/q41/p1", "position": "The Prophet's presence and aspiration convey tranquility and purify egoic attachment.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says wealth fuels desires and spiritual training first weakens them; his attention and companionship bring a settled light to the heart. Al-Sulamī reports turning hearts from the world toward the afterlife."}, {"id": "9:103/q41/p2", "position": "True repentance requires admission, humility, tears, forgiveness-seeking, and leaving deliberate sin.", "reasons": "Al-Bursevī treats confession as Adam's legacy, reports his two hundred years of weeping, cites Ḥāfiẓ's verse on Adam's sin, urges blessings upon the Prophet and prayer for believers, defines divine forgiveness as concealment, and says mistakes and forgetfulness are pardoned."}]}

{"id": "11:41/q08", "question": "What grammatical role does “in God's name” play?", "turns_on": "The syntactic governor, whether the wording is one sentence or two, and whether a circumstantial clause has a pronoun linking it to its subject.", "positions": [{"id": "11:41/q08/p1", "position": "It is circumstantial to the riders: they board naming God.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī compares 5:61; al-Ālūsī calls bāʾ accompaniment or supplies “saying.” The sailing and mooring words are times of the invocation, not times to embark, as Makkī stresses."}, {"id": "11:41/q08/p2", "position": "It forms a complete nominal sentence: the ark's sailing and mooring are by God's name.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and Ibn al-Anbārī make bi the predicate and the nouns subjects; al-Naḥḥās also reports an omitted mawḍiʿ. {"id": "11:41/q12", "question": "What is meant by God's “name” in the expression?", "turns_on": "Whether ism contributes independently to the phrase or is syntactically inserted.", "positions": [{"id": "11:41/q12/p1", "position": "“Name” is an inserted word, so the expression means “by God.”", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī cites a poetic line, “Then the name of peace be upon you both”; al-Ālūsī cites Labīd and understands divine power, command or permission."}, {"id": "11:41/q12/p2", "position": "The divine name Allah is God's greatest name.", "reasons": "Jābir ibn Zayd argues it precedes every other name throughout the Qur'an; al-Ḍaḥḥāk assigns the basmala's letters to splendor, glory and sovereignty, and says Allah is creation's deity."}, {"id": "11:41/q12/p3", "position": "The alif of ism is omitted in the written basmala through frequent use.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports the outward scholars' majority restriction: omission occurs when ism follows bāʾ and is annexed to Allah."}]}
{"id": "11:41/q13", "question": "What alternative wording of the invocation is reported?", "turns_on": "Different transmitted wording.", "positions": [{"id": "11:41/q13/p1", "position": "Ubayy's codex has “ʿalā ismi Allāh” instead of “bi-smi Allāh.”", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports the codex wording."}, {"id": "11:41/q13/p2", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd recited wording referring to its sailing and anchoring.", "reasons": "Al-Durr preserves the variant without further linguistic argument."}]}
{"id": "11:41/q14", "question": "How are the vowels and forms of “its sailing and mooring” read?", "turns_on": "The mīm vowels distinguish causative and basic verb patterns; the participial forms name God as agent, and reciters also vary imāla and following vowels.", "positions": [{"id": "11:41/q14/p1", "position": "Both initial mīms have ḍamma, yielding causative verbal nouns.", "reasons": "Attributed to the Medinan, Meccan, Basran and many named readers; Abū ʿUbayd and Abū Ḥātim prefer it. Al-Thaʿlabī compares 12:67 and 17:80; al-Baghawī adds 23:29. Ibn ʿAṭiyya cites Labīd. Some reports differ on the following rāʾ and sīn. Al-Burṣawī says the a/u forms of majrāhā are synonymous verbal nouns and the u-form of mursāhā denotes coming to rest."}, {"id": "11:41/q14/p2", "position": "Majrāhā has fatḥa on mīm, with kasra or imāla at rāʾ; mursāhā has ḍamma on mīm.", "reasons": "Attributed to Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ and others. Abū Razīn and Abū al-Mutawakkil have fatḥa on rāʾ. Ibn Masʿūd has imāla. Qirāʾāt-Er identifies imāla as a dialectal tilt."}, {"id": "11:41/q14/p3", "position": "Both initial mīms have fatḥa, deriving from the simple verbs for sailing and settling.", "reasons": "Attributed variously to Ibn Muḥayṣin, Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb, al-Aʿmash, Ibn Masʿūd and others; reports differ on imāla and the following consonant vowels. Al-Thaʿlabī cites an Imruʾ al-Qays line for the noun pattern; al-Ṭabarī cites ʿAntarah's tarsū. Several sources say the nouns can denote action, time, or place."}, {"id": "11:41/q14/p4", "position": "Both words are active participles, mujrihā and mursīhā, describing God as the one who causes sailing and mooring.", "reasons": "Reported from Abū Rajāʾ, Mujāhid and other readers; some lists include al-Nakhaʿī, al-Jaḥdarī, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan and Qatāda. Qirāʾāt-Er stresses divine agency and reports a variant with imāla. Al-Zajjāj calls the form linguistically possible but not a transmitted recitation in his assessment."}, {"id": "11:41/q14/p5", "position": "Different canonical reciters vary the imāla or openness of the following consonants while retaining the reported mīm readings.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī says Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥafṣ open sīn; Nāfiʿ and Abū Bakr use an intermediate vowel, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf incline it. Abū ʿImrān and Ibn Jubayr raise both mīms with open rāʾ and sīn; al-Nasafī reports Abū ʿAmr with kasra on rāʾ."}]}
{"id": "11:41/q15", "question": "How are the active-participle forms parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether annexed participles can be definite enough to modify God, or instead require apposition, an implied subject, or accusative syntax.", "positions": [{"id": "11:41/q15/p1", "position": "They are genitive attributes of God.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī considers genitive likelier than circumstantial accusative; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū al-Baqāʾ use adjective analysis. Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī object that the future participle's annexation remains indefinite, unless it becomes definite as al-Khalīl permits in some cases."}, {"id": "11:41/q15/p2", "position": "They are appositions or predicate substitutes for God's name.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān favors predicate substitutes over indefinite adjectives; al-Samīn calls them appositions and al-Ālūsī finds badal sounder."}, {"id": "11:41/q15/p3", "position": "They are nominative after an omitted “He.”", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī allow an implicit huwa."}, {"id": "11:41/q15/p4", "position": "They are accusative circumstantial modifiers, or an accusative of praise.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī allow the circumstantial case; al-Zajjāj gives the praise parse, and Makkī calls his estimated circumstantial analysis difficult."}]}
{"id": "11:41/q16", "question": "What does “its sailing” denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the form names an action or its causation, and whether a verbal noun also serves as a time or place noun.", "positions": [{"id": "11:41/q16/p1", "position": "The ark's running, course, or journey.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda adduces Labīd's mujra Dāḥis as a race or course; Ibn Qutayba and al-Ṭabarī use passage. Ibn al-Jawzī reports Abū Manṣūr's causative versus intransitive distinction; Qirāʾāt-Er notes a passive nuance of divine causation."}, {"id": "11:41/q16/p3", "position": "It can name the place or time of the ark's movement.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās calls it the place in the water where the ship runs; al-Kashshāf and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ allow a place, and grammarians also make it a time noun."}]}
{"id": "11:41/q17", "question": "What does “its mooring” denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the noun points to rest itself, its location, or the act of making the vessel rest.", "positions": [{"id": "11:41/q17/p1", "position": "The ark's coming to rest, stopping, or place of anchoring.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba give the stopping place; Ibn ʿAbbās says where it rests in water. {"id": "11:41/q18", "question": "What syntactic role can “its sailing and mooring” take?", "turns_on": "Whether the nouns are raised by the prepositional predicate, made accusative as time or place, or replace an omitted place noun.", "positions": [{"id": "11:41/q18/p1", "position": "They are nominative subjects whose predicate is “in God's name.”", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Naḥḥās allow subject status; Ibn al-Anbārī says bi serves as predicate while the sense is “by God's name.” Al-Fārisī compares maqām as action or place of iqāma; al-Ālūsī describes coordinated subjects and an omitted predicate."}, {"id": "11:41/q18/p2", "position": "They are accusative adverbs of time or place, or verbal nouns with an omitted “time.”", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ omits the preposition, giving “at its sailing and settling.” Al-Fārisī says the two inevitable periods cannot govern boarding. Makkī gives the implied stability in bismillāh as governor, not “board.” Al-Ālūsī reports objection that a bounded place needs fī, with a response that the phrase remains open."}, {"id": "11:41/q18/p3", "position": "An omitted “place” is understood, with majrāhā standing for the place of its movement.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās explicitly supplies mawḍiʿ before omission; the source's argument is ellipsis."}]}
{"id": "11:41/q19", "question": "Who rode in the ark, and how many?", "turns_on": "The divergent numbers in transmitted reports.", "positions": [{"id": "11:41/q19/p1", "position": "Eight people: Noah, his wife, three sons, and their three wives.", "reasons": "Abū Ṣāliḥ names the sons Japheth, Ham and Sam."}, {"id": "11:41/q19/p2", "position": "Eighty men with their families.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives a 150-day voyage in the same report; al-Qurṭubī transmits an upper deck with forty men and forty women, with animals on lower levels."}]}
